metadata.title: Right Answer, Wrong Chain
metadata.subject: Process supervision and multi-hop agents — what outcome grading cannot see
metadata.primary_sources: Trivedi, Balasubramanian, Khot, Sabharwal — “MuSiQue: Multihop Questions via Single-hop Question Composition”, TACL (DOI 10.1162/tacl_a_00475); Lightman, Kosaraju, Burda, Edwards, Baker, Lee, Leike, Schulman, Sutskever, Cobbe — “Let's Verify Step by Step”, arXiv 2305.20050
metadata.title_note: Commissioned as “Process-Supervised & Multi-Hop AI Agents”, with permission to retitle. That phrase joins a SUPERVISION METHOD to a TASK TYPE as though they were one subject. B01 separates them and names the measured failure that actually connects them — a correct answer produced from a chain that was never followed.
metadata.note: ai-explainer spine, claude-hai channel, Weekly STEM. FRAMEWORK: three questions — WHAT COUNTS AS A STEP / WHO LABELLED THE STEPS / IS THE ADVANTAGE FUNDAMENTAL OR PRACTICAL. Falsifiability beat is B06: an earlier study found parity on grade-school maths, and a theoretical result holds that outcome supervision is no more statistically difficult than process supervision under standard coverage assumptions — so the advantage may be practical rather than informational. B07's claim about agent step labels is argued from the verified contrast (800k human labels for maths; no comparable public corpus for agent steps) and is marked in FACTCHECK.md as reasoning, not a cited empirical finding. DiRe figures read from the MuSiQue PDF directly. See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane. Process supervision and multi-hop agents are two different things — one is how you grade, the other is what you asked. They belong in the same sentence for exactly one reason, and it is a measured one: on the benchmarks built to test multi-step reasoning, you can score well without doing the reasoning.

beats.role_note: premise — two different things, and the one measured fact that joins them
beats.narration_text: First, what the phrase actually joins. Process supervision is a way of grading: you score every intermediate step instead of only the final answer. Multi-hop is a kind of question: one that cannot be answered without chaining several facts together. Those are not the same category. The reason they get said together is a failure mode — a model producing the right answer from a chain that was never actually followed. Outcome grading, by construction, cannot tell the difference.
beats.new_visual_element: the two halves, separated, then joined by the failure

shot.show: grading method and question type as separate cards, joined by one shared failure
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered cards side by side: PROCESS SUPERVISION labelled 'how you grade', MULTI-HOP labelled 'what you asked'. Beneath, spanning both, a terracotta card reading 'right answer, chain never followed' with connectors rising to each.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any process-supervision claim, AS A STRUCTURE first
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any claim that grading the steps works better. One: what counts as a step — because in arithmetic a step is a checkable object, and in an agent trajectory it is whatever you decided to cut on. Two: who labelled the steps — a human, or a process that inferred the labels from how things turned out. Three: is the advantage fundamental or practical — because those have different consequences for whether it will hold in your setting.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT COUNTS AS A STEP / WHO LABELLED THEM / FUNDAMENTAL OR PRACTICAL
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The second lands in terracotta — it is the question that decides whether process supervision is really process supervision — and the rest of the reel is scored against all three.

beats.role_note: the failure mode, quantified — the DiRe scores from the MuSiQue paper
beats.narration_text: Here is the measurement that makes this concrete. There is a probe called disconnected reasoning: you split the supporting evidence so no single piece can answer the question, and you see how well a model still does. On HotpotQA, a model scores sixty-eight point eight answer F1 while bypassing the reasoning steps. On two-wiki, sixty-three point four. On MuSiQue, a dataset built specifically to resist shortcuts, thirty-seven point eight. Lower is harder to cheat.
beats.new_visual_element: the three DiRe scores, with direction stated

shot.show: HotpotQA 68.8 / 2Wiki 63.4 / MuSiQue 37.8, lower is harder to cheat
shot.visual_intent: Three horizontal bars, proportional, each with its dataset name on the left and the figure on the right. HotpotQA longest, in terracotta because the headline is that a reasoning benchmark can be scored on without reasoning. MuSiQue shortest, in ink. A caption reads 'lower is harder to cheat'. Citation strip names the paper and venue.

beats.role_note: the second tell — performance against hop count, and the model that does not move
beats.narration_text: There is a second tell in the same paper, and it is subtler. Their best model scores fifty-seven point nine on two-hop questions, forty-seven point nine on three-hop, and twenty-eight point one on four-hop — it degrades as the chain gets longer, which is what actually doing the chain looks like. Another model stays at roughly forty-two percent no matter how many hops the question needs. A flat line across hop count is not robustness. It is a model that is not hopping.
beats.new_visual_element: degradation with hops, against a flat line

shot.visual_intent: A small two-series chart: three descending bars labelled 2-hop, 3-hop, 4-hop in ink with their figures, and beside them three equal bars in terracotta all labelled about 42%. A caption under the flat series reads 'not robustness — not hopping'. Cited.

beats.role_note: process supervision — what it is and the one result everyone cites
beats.narration_text: So that is the problem. Process supervision is the proposed answer: grade every intermediate step rather than the final answer alone, and stop at the first step that is wrong. The paper everyone cites reports a process-supervised model solving seventy-eight percent of problems from a representative subset of the MATH test set, and says process supervision significantly outperforms outcome supervision. What that took is the number worth remembering: eight hundred thousand step-level labels, written by humans.
beats.new_visual_element: the method, the result, and its cost

shot.show: 78% on a MATH subset, and PRM800K at 800,000 human step labels
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered stat cards: 78% captioned 'of a representative MATH subset', and 800,000 captioned 'step-level labels, written by humans' in terracotta. Beneath, one line describing the method: grade each step, stop at the first wrong one. Citation strip names authors and arXiv id.

beats.role_note: it is not a law — an earlier parity result and a theoretical one
beats.narration_text: Now the part that keeps this honest, because process supervision is not a law. An earlier study on grade-school maths found outcome and process supervision reaching similar final performance — so the advantage is not universal across difficulty. And a theoretical result goes further: under standard assumptions about data coverage, learning from outcomes is no harder statistically than learning from steps, up to polynomial factors. If that holds, the gain is not information. It is practical — which is still worth having, and is a different claim.

shot.show: parity on easier maths, and the statistical result
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered rows. The first: parity on grade-school maths, in soft ink. The second, terracotta: outcome supervision is no more statistically difficult, up to polynomial factors in horizon. Beneath, one line: 'then the advantage is practical, not informational'. Cited to both.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 2 — what breaks when you move from maths to agents
beats.narration_text: Which brings us to the question that decides whether any of this transfers. In arithmetic, a step is a checkable object: a human can look at one line and say whether it follows. In an agent trajectory, a step is whatever you decided to cut on — a tool call, a thought, a retrieval — and whether it was correct often is not knowable until the end. Eight hundred thousand human labels existed for maths. There is no comparable public corpus for agent steps, and when labels are inferred from how the episode turned out, outcome information has come back in under a new name.
beats.new_visual_element: the two senses of step, and the labelling problem

shot.show: a checkable maths step beside an agent step whose correctness is not local
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered panels. Left, 'a step in arithmetic': one line, checkable by a human, in ink. Right, 'a step in an agent run': a tool call whose correctness is not knowable yet, in terracotta. Beneath, a chip reading '800,000 human labels existed for one of these'.

beats.role_note: the rubric scored, then the two-sided verdict
beats.narration_text: Scored. What counts as a step: clear in maths, a design decision in an agent. Who labelled them: humans, eight hundred thousand times, for the result everyone quotes. Fundamental or practical: the theory says the information is not the bottleneck. So — be excited that there is now a measured way to catch a right answer built on a broken chain, and that the benchmarks have started being rebuilt around it. Be sceptical of process supervision claimed for an agent without saying what a step is and who decided it was correct.
beats.new_visual_element: the rubric answered, then the two-sided verdict

shot.show: three rubric rows answered, then BE EXCITED ABOUT / BE SCEPTICAL OF
shot.visual_intent: Three label-and-chip rows score the rubric. Beneath, two lines: BE EXCITED ABOUT in ink, BE SCEPTICAL OF in terracotta.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the next agent-evaluation claim, with GOOD/BAD
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time you read that an agent was trained or evaluated with process supervision, ask three things: what one step was, who labelled it correct, and whether that label could have been known before the episode ended. If the answer to the third is no, you are reading outcome supervision with extra steps.
